newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo brokers seek safeguards ahead of privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Yugo brokers seek safeguards ahead of privatisation.

text.p: Yugoslav brokers called on their guild on Tuesday to protect them from being manipulated in the forthcoming privatisation process.

"Without a strong professional organisation it will be difficult for brokers to resist pressures and manipulation in the privatisation process and development of the financial market," spokesman of the Belgrade bourse Milko Stimac said.
"It's not difficult to imagine how easily brokers can be manipulated. They need protection just like lawyers," he said.
A privatisation law is expected to be adopted by the government by the end of June to put small and medium-sized companies up for sale. A large slice of Serbian industry is currently in state hands.
Brokers feared they could be used for insider trading and simply driven away when the sale is over.
"The bourse is there to protect from market risks but this guild must protect from non-market risks," Stimac told Reuters.
Marking the first anniversary of the club gathering 138 members, brokers said they could play a more important role in financial market regulations and the privatisation process.

"We hope this guild can become an almost equal partner in creating new laws regulating the financial market. We should have a place in the process, our ideas can be useful," Dusko Susnjar, secretary of the Yugoslav Brokers Association, said.
Susnjar insisted Yugoslav laws regulating financial markets were incomplete although the government adopted laws on banks, enterprises, brokerages, securities.
To bring the legal framework in line with western standards Yugoslav lawmakers needed to update existing laws with a document on investment funds before privatisation starts.
Ivan Maricic, broker with the Belgrade bourse, appealed to brokers to push for diversification of instruments traded on the bourse.

"We still trade the same instruments just like we did three years ago. Apart from (central bank) bonds we have developed almost no other instrument. We haven't even influenced any changes in maturity of the paper," Maricic said.

Two official bourses in Belgrade and Podgorica trade mainly in commercial paper and treasury bills. The central bank has been selling its short-term bonds to drain liquidity from the market but failed to launch new forms of its market operations.
Most instruments mature in no more than 30 days.
Apart from those, the market sees an occasional sale of certificates of deposit and some seasonal activity in forward contracts selling agricultural produce.
Although officially called stock exchanges, both the Belgrade and the Montenegro bourses have hardly seen any trade in shares in the past two years to justify their names.

Analysts saw privatisation as a precondition for developing a real equities market. But while waiting for privatisation to begin the bourses were trying to grab any market activity under their umbrella to help establish a habit of market trading.

Brokers said the announced privatisation law in Serbia and a government plan to release frozen hard currency savings by issuing bonds could help develop secondary trading but feared those laws would not be implemented in the near future.
"Such laws are a matter of political will and a part of political marketing in an election year," a broker said.
But Maricic insisted brokers could do more other than wait for the state to begin with reforms.

"The overall economic and financial situation is fairly stable. We must become more active in advising our clients how to deal with financial problems. Depending on how inventive and successful we are, the market will develop," he said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
